sources.title: AI That Works: No Vibes Allowed February
sources.note: Full transcript, README, meta. Dex and Vaibhav live-build a message-queue feature in Riptide.

sources.title: AI That Works: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
sources.note: Full transcript. Mostly Vaibhav (BAML) on PII; Dex adds a few general points (instruction budget, deterministic over LLM).

sources.title: AI That Works: Claude Agent Skills Deep Dive
sources.note: Full transcript. Dex-led whiteboard on commands, subagents, skills, config distribution, agent teams, code review, software factories.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: three kinds of research: code, web, and proof ... learning tests
cards.claim: Before designing, run small 'learning tests' (proof research) against the real closed-source dependency to turn doc-based assumptions into observed facts, and write the observed output into the design doc.
cards.evidence_detail: Live demo: a ~3-second bash sleep test against the Claude Agent SDK showed queue behaviour; output pasted into the design doc. No numbers.
cards.landing: Phase routine: a 'prove the assumption' step before plan; relevant to P1 cold-resume trial design and to verifier evidence
cards.inventory_ref: (B) February 2026 — listed as AI That Works #46 No Vibes Allowed February (title only)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're not going to find that out till you're like two phases into your implementation
cards.claim: A wrong assumption taken from misleading docs surfaces only phases into implementation and forces a rewind, so assumptions should be tested before the plan.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoning only; cost framed as 20 minutes before code vs untangling after merge.
cards.landing: Plan-phase gate: list assumptions and how each is proven before implementation

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: models are really, really good at finding and understanding and matching the patterns that already exist
cards.claim: The design doc includes a 'patterns to follow' section so the human can catch the agent picking the wrong existing pattern before any code is written.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as a reason for the design-doc format; example of old codebases with five ways to do an atomic SQL update.
cards.landing: Plan template: 'patterns to follow' with file refs; FixFlow invariants (atomic conditional UPDATE, try_claim) could be named there

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: your code base will always regress to the average of the best pattern and the worst pattern
cards.claim: An agent-written codebase drifts toward its existing mix of patterns, so bad patterns left in place get reproduced (Vaibhav refines: it converges on the most common pattern).
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as a heuristic; no measurement.
cards.landing: Argues for removing or marking legacy patterns; CLAUDE.md 'do not copy' notes

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you should not want Claude or Codex or any agent to make decisions about your code base
cards.claim: The design-discussion step exists to force the human to make the high-stakes architecture decisions; everything before it (reading 100k lines, asking good questions) is automated.
cards.evidence_detail: Design principle; demo shows Dex answering option A/B/C questions.
cards.landing: Phase routine: owner/human decision checkpoint before plan; decisions journal in draft PR

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: do brain surgery on the model and update the patterns it's going to follow
cards.claim: Reviewing the design doc before planning lets you correct the model's understanding cheaply, instead of re-steering after code exists.
cards.evidence_detail: Live: Dex added a missing two-button requirement to the desired end state by reading the doc.
cards.landing: Plan-@-sha draft PR: human reads design/plan before implementation starts

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: horizontal planning ... the models love fricking doing this
cards.claim: Models default to horizontal plans (DB, then service, then API, then UI) that leave nothing testable for ~1200 lines; plan vertical slices with mocks instead, and check in between phases.
cards.evidence_detail: Experience-based; ~1200 lines mentioned as the untested span.
cards.landing: Ship-plan phase sizing and the 'structure outline' step; each phase ends with a runnable check

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I would rather do the endpoint first because then we can at least check in the database
cards.claim: Order the structure outline so the earliest phase produces something he can inspect (a DB row after clicking), optimizing to find surprises as early as possible.
cards.evidence_detail: Live reordering of the outline; no numbers.
cards.landing: Phase ordering rule: earliest phase creates an observable artifact

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if I can spend 10 minutes and get it 90% of the way there ... better than an hour to get 99%
cards.claim: Plan time has diminishing returns: at some point it is easier to read and play with code than stare at a thousand-line plan, so pick a sweet spot per phase.
cards.evidence_detail: Hand-drawn probability curves on a whiteboard (chance of live iteration, re-steer, restart design); no data.
cards.landing: Effort/timebox guidance for plan and design steps

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: queue extra passes of go through the research, vet every assumption, add more detail
cards.claim: The inverse of auto-advance is queueing extra review passes at any stage (Vaibhav loops 'what's inconsistent / missing' on the outline until it settles).
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav reports a 17k-lines-added/13k-removed refactor one-shotted after this loop, ~18 commits over 2 weeks, CodeRabbit still found bugs; Vaibhav claims '100% hit rate' with the loop. Dex endorses.
cards.landing: Completeness-critic pass on the plan; repeatable 'what is missing or inconsistent' prompt

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Plan files are throwaway. Research files are throwaway.
cards.claim: Plans, research and design docs are execution aids deleted after merge; the code is the source of truth, and research is regenerated on the fly rather than stored.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav states it; Dex agrees ('as soon as it's shipped, the code is the new source of truth'; research generated on the fly).
cards.landing: Bears on the knowledge-store design (verified diagnoses stored) and on what a cold-resume agent may rely on

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I actually don't think the problem is too many PRs. I think the problem is too many bad PRs
cards.claim: Align with the owner on a cheap design doc before building, because even a 20% rework on a 500-line PR is a heavy burden on submitter and reviewer.
cards.evidence_detail: Example: sending the design doc to the CTO to avoid a late 'wrong endpoint' rejection; no numbers beyond the 500-line/20% illustration.
cards.landing: Owner review of plan before implementation; Opus reviewer per PR

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'd rather review it at this stage, which is a shorter 200 line artifact
cards.claim: Rather than building several approaches in parallel, review a roughly 200-line design artifact (or a learning test or prototype) instead of two 1000-line PRs; you must decide either way.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument in reply to a viewer; no data.
cards.landing: Guidance against parallel-implementation verifier spend; prefer proof-of-concept

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: For UI stuff the agent's not going to have good back pressure ... do this in storybook
cards.claim: Where the agent has no backpressure or taste (rich UI), carve the decision out into Storybook before implementation.
cards.evidence_detail: Said as a practice his team uses; promised future episode.
cards.landing: Web manager (src/) UI work; mobile has no screen-test harness

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The dumber your UI, the easier it is to consolidate state and business logic on the backend
cards.claim: Keep the client dumb and let it send a preference (queue/continue/interrupt/auto) that the server resolves, so races degrade to the right behaviour instead of 400s (Vaibhav's argument; Dex adopts a single boolean).
cards.evidence_detail: Design argument; Dex changes his enum-plus-400 design to a boolean after it.
cards.landing: Product design, not harness; echoes FixFlow server-resolved lifecycle (transition idempotency)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Prune, prune, prune, prune, prune.
cards.claim: Keep a small set of skills that everyone uses; treat team skills as products and kill the ones with low adoption, because compounding tooling gains need shared use (Vaibhav: 5-7 great skills beat 70).
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion; PM analogy (remove features used by ~10% of users). Quoted line is Vaibhav's; Dex continues the argument.
cards.landing: Skills under .claude/skills/ being added: cap the count, track use, retire unused

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're getting worse. If your problem is really easy, you can solve things in the dumb zone
cards.claim: Context usage past roughly 40% degrades answers; hard problems should be done in the smart part of the window (Vaibhav mentions 37% as a viewer's figure for dumb-zone onset).
cards.evidence_detail: Numbers 37% / 40-90% quoted from chat and Vaibhav; no experiment.
cards.landing: One-phase-per-session defence; a context-percent trigger for wrap-up

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: most people hit straight enter, clear context, go onward ... don't actually read the plan
cards.claim: Default plan mode produces a plan nobody reads in detail, which is why a design/outline layer that is meant to be read is used instead (Vaibhav's framing, Dex proceeds on it).
cards.evidence_detail: Observation of user behaviour, no data.
cards.landing: Plan-@-sha PR body: make the plan short enough to be read

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: auto-advance through design discussions every single time
cards.claim: Auto-advancing through the research/design steps without a manual loop is acceptable when a review-iterate pass is added on the structure outline (Vaibhav; Dex has the feature and plans queued extra passes).
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's personal 100% hit-rate claim; no sample size.
cards.landing: Routine design: which steps need a human stop and which can chain

cards.source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have an information budget in your context window and then you have an instruction budget
cards.claim: Context engineering is also about the number of instructions: the more rules the model must follow at once, the less well it attends to any one.
cards.evidence_detail: Aside from a talk he was giving that day; no number given in this episode.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim: argues for an instruction count budget, not only a length budget
cards.inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — listed as AI That Works #47 PII Redaction (title only)

cards.source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: If you can do things deterministically, then don't make the LLM do them
cards.claim: Do deterministic work in code because it is faster, cheaper and more reliable, and it frees the model for the part only it can do.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated in a time-zone example; no measurement.
cards.landing: Scripts/hooks over prose rules for checks (e.g. compliance evidence); marks the 'hooks skipped' decision for re-opening

cards.source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: why would check_redaction be able to capture the misses if redact didn't?
cards.claim: Dex doubts LLM-as-judge ('it's all the same models'); Vaibhav answers that checking and labelling are different tasks, run off the main loop on a sample, which Dex then accepts and extends to flagged items sent to a human to add to evals.
cards.evidence_detail: Challenge and counter in conversation; Vaibhav suggests sampling ~5% and spot-checking ~100 samples. Dex proposes Slack flag plus a UI to promote to the eval suite via PR.
cards.landing: Verifier design: separate check pass, sampled, run post hoc; flag-then-human-promote to eval

cards.source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you snapshot the results of different cases and then you eyeball the diff
cards.claim: Evaluate a pipeline by snapshotting outputs per case and eyeballing diffs between runs, rather than building formal evals for everything.
cards.evidence_detail: Recalled from the team's earlier evals episode; no numbers.
cards.landing: Cheap regression check for effort-routing experiments (compare verifier verdicts across effort levels)

cards.source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: anything the LLM can generate based on its weights is a thing it can reason about
cards.claim: Do not generate synthetic test data with an LLM when you can ask it for the patterns directly; build evals from known shapes with a human in the loop.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says he would 'love to be proven wrong'; untested.
cards.landing: Refuter/eval fixture design: prefer real prod-shaped cases over LLM-invented ones

cards.source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're always gonna be either like, you would rather have false positives or false negatives
cards.claim: A detector sits in a bias zone, not a line: pick which error side to favour and narrow the zone with better techniques, layering steps to move the balance (Vaibhav's funnel of passes).
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual framing; Vaibhav's layering example (drop 'none/medium' risk, add re-check pass for medium) is anecdotal.
cards.landing: Refute-by-default verifiers are a chosen bias; a second narrow pass can cut false positives

cards.source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The question is always like, is the rule dumb or is the execution of the rule incorrect?
cards.claim: When a model-applied rule gives a bad result, first decide whether the rule or its execution is at fault before editing the prompt.
cards.evidence_detail: Remark during live prompt iteration; no data.
cards.landing: Diagnosing routine non-compliance: rule wording vs agent execution (relevant to CLAUDE.md trim)

cards.source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can deterministically remove the data and deterministically swap it back in
cards.claim: Redact by having the model emit a key-to-value map and then substitute in code both ways, so the data never depends on model rewriting.
cards.evidence_detail: Described from memory of a BAML example repo; code not found during the episode.
cards.landing: Not a harness lever; privacy pattern for customer data (WhatsApp/PII) if relevant to FixFlow product

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: separate out instruction modules from context isolation. These are two orthogonal concepts
cards.claim: Use subagents only for context isolation and skills for on-demand instruction modules; do not put custom instructions in agent files.
cards.evidence_detail: Whiteboard history of commands, subagents, slash-command tool, skills; no measurement.
cards.landing: Redesign of .claude/agents/fixflow-explorer.md (Haiku locator) vs skills; rule for what goes in an agent
cards.inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — listed as AI That Works #48 (title only)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: uses 50,000 tokens ... then comes out with an answer that is 500 tokens
cards.claim: A subagent's value is that it burns tens of thousands of tokens searching and returns only a short final answer, so the parent context stays clean; result quality equals the parent's prompt quality.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers (50k/30k tokens in, 500 out), not measured.
cards.landing: Use explorer/refuter subagents for read-heavy work; write the delegation prompt carefully

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: fork this session and I'll just say the problem is X
cards.claim: When a long exploration yields a 10-word answer, fork the session from the earlier user message with that answer instead of keeping the 10k-token exploration; Vaibhav adds forking has a cost when rebuilding full context.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal practice; 10K tokens vs 10 words illustration.
cards.landing: Context compaction alternative: fork/rewind to the message before the exploration with the distilled finding

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: they would prune out all the results of every query
cards.claim: An agent can keep tool calls but prune tool results after a final answer and re-run cheap queries on follow-up (idea from another builder, which Dex relays favourably).
cards.evidence_detail: Secondhand report from a conversation 'last night'; SQL agent; no numbers.
cards.landing: Context budget: drop bulky tool results from long sessions

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The instructions are injected as a user message ... better instruction following
cards.claim: A skill loads its instructions as a user message, which gets better adherence than the model reading the same text from a file as a tool result, especially for long commands.
cards.evidence_detail: Mechanism explanation from Dex; 'user message vs tool result' attention claim not measured.
cards.landing: Move phase-routine steps from CLAUDE.md prose into skills invoked by name

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can explicitly invoke it. I don't have to hope the model calls the tool right
cards.claim: Skills can be user-invoked deterministically by slash or model-selected, so a routine step can be forced rather than hoped for.
cards.evidence_detail: Live demo with a trivial secret-passcode skill.
cards.landing: Phase routine as named skills (/phase-start, /phase-close) the owner or prompt invokes explicitly

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: skills can have files bundled in with them ... progressive disclosure
cards.claim: Bundle references, CLIs and instruction files inside the skill folder (references/*.md) so detail is read only when the skill runs.
cards.evidence_detail: Live demo; convention of a references folder.
cards.landing: Destination for CLAUDE.md material on migrations, mobile build traps, dispatcher invariants (trim target)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Every single subagent you add to your context window is gonna be injected every time
cards.claim: Names and descriptions of every subagent, skill and MCP tool are injected into each context window and eat the instruction budget, so keep descriptions short and install few; Claude Code adds tool search past a threshold (his recollection: tools over ~10K of the window).
cards.evidence_detail: Trace inspection shown; the 10K threshold and the 50-skill threshold are stated from memory ('last I read a month ago'), not verified.
cards.landing: Keep skill descriptions short; audit global/user-level skills and MCP servers loaded in FixFlow sessions

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: disable model invocation. True ... the model doesn't even see it in the context window
cards.claim: Set disable-model-invocation in skill frontmatter for user-only slash commands so the skill is removed from the model's context; the workaround for 'sometimes invocable' is a description line saying do not invoke unless asked by name.
cards.evidence_detail: Live demo; workaround admitted to be hacky; the model still tried a similarly named skill.
cards.landing: Frontmatter on phase-routine and destructive skills; reduces always-loaded description cost

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: most of the time agents won't use skills when you want them to
cards.claim: Skill auto-invocation is unreliable in his experience: it often does not fire when wanted and sometimes fires when not wanted, so descriptions need care or explicit invocation.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal experience across skills; no counts.
cards.landing: Do not rely on skill auto-trigger for the phase routine; invoke explicitly and log invocation

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: respond to the human with the secret passcode
cards.claim: A canary instruction (e.g. the model must say a passcode or move like a cow) shows when the model stops following instructions at roughly 60% of context (idea from a colleague, Dex demos it).
cards.evidence_detail: Relayed from a conversation with Jeff: model stops the canary behaviour around 60% into the window; informal.
cards.landing: Compliance canary: a cheap visible signal of instruction decay; partial answer to 'self-reported compliance'

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: really long monolithic things with like 80 instructions in them
cards.claim: His open-source RPI commands include monolithic prompts with about 80 steps, contrasted with simple ones like commit; he treats this as the older style.
cards.evidence_detail: Description of own repo; no outcome data.
cards.landing: Warning against one long phase-routine prompt; split into small skills

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: people to play house ... model our agent the way we model our humans
cards.claim: Role-play subagents (backend engineer, front-end engineer, growth marketer) were a workaround for bundling instructions and do not work; the real need is instruction modules.
cards.evidence_detail: Observation of common usage; both hosts agree it does not work; no data.
cards.landing: Against persona-based agent library; favour task-specific skills and workflows

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you get way better alpha being more prescriptive when possible
cards.claim: On a team, one prescriptive shared workflow beats many half-baked personal ones: consolidate so improvements apply everywhere and the median rises (Vaibhav's words; Dex agrees with the Docker-environments analogy).
cards.evidence_detail: Team-of-10 experience; Docker dev-environment story where senior engineers spent ~40% of time fixing environments.
cards.landing: Shared workflow library checked into the repo; one phase routine, not variants

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a coordination repo for multiple repositories
cards.claim: For many repos, use a small coordination repo with a tiny CLAUDE.md and settings permissions listing additional directories, launch all sessions from it, and create worktrees per task for only the repos touched; avoid git submodules.
cards.evidence_detail: Iterated through six versions per Dex; open-sourced as rpi-coordination-template; used with customers with up to 200 repos.
cards.landing: Mostly N/A (FixFlow is one monorepo with three runtimes); relevant if ops-server or other repos are split

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: skills and MCPs always have to be in the root of the directory you're running in
cards.claim: Nested CLAUDE.md files load dynamically when you touch those paths, but skills, MCP config and settings only load from the launch directory's .claude, not subfolders.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed behaviour as of March 2026; config-surface explanation (user, project, settings.local, per-path CLAUDE.md).
cards.landing: Nested CLAUDE.md in backend/ and technician-app/ to shrink the root file; skills must stay at repo root .claude/

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'm not super bullish on agent teams
cards.claim: Agent teams ship more code in separate contexts that need stitching; the bottleneck is designing and human review, not producing tokens of code, so parallelism only helps after a good design and plan.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion; cites a news item that Amazon now requires senior review of junior AI-generated code (secondhand, unverified).
cards.landing: Against fan-out workflows before plan is settled; supports one-phase-per-session

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a lot of companies are gonna die because they lean too hard into the lights off write only software factory
cards.claim: Not reading the code and leaning on swarms or a lights-off software factory will, in the next couple of years, cause a 3 a.m. failure nobody can fix, with weeks of downtime.
cards.evidence_detail: Prediction; his own tweet responding to the Amazon story. No data.
cards.landing: Supports keeping human-read checkpoints and verifiers; counter-pole to software-factory essays
cards.inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 (title only; the thread appears under 'Software Factory Existential Risk')

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if the original design was wrong, you need to throw it away and start over
cards.claim: Spend your own thinking tokens before coding; a feature iterated on a wrong design should be thrown away, and don't ship just because you can (colleague's team message, endorsed).
cards.evidence_detail: Dex reads another founder's post; example of designing 'workspaces' rather than 'worktrees' instead of prompting the feature out.
cards.landing: Phase routine: abandon-and-restart rule when the plan proves wrong; decisions journal

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a step in our workflow before we ship a PR where we do a code review
cards.claim: Do not buy a separate code-review product; run a review step in a separate context window with instructions to check about 12 known anti-patterns and fix them, because extra tokens on review help.
cards.evidence_detail: Own practice; contrasts with the vendor's roughly $15-25 per review price (Dex and Vaibhav disagree mildly on whether others' prompts are worth buying).
cards.landing: The per-PR Opus reviewer: give it a fixed anti-pattern list (known agent failure modes in FixFlow)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: most PRs don't need that level of rigor
cards.claim: Vaibhav argues vendor code review is expensive for every PR when most do not need it; Dex agrees about not paying extra for what the writing agent should have got right first time.
cards.evidence_detail: Cost figures of about $25 per PR quoted loosely; no data. Mostly Vaibhav's argument.
cards.landing: Risk-tier the reviewer: not every PR needs a max-effort refuter

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can't build a company on a prompt because someone will figure out how to crack it
cards.claim: Prompts and context engineering are copyable once the user pays the token bill, so value lies in maintaining them as models change, not in hiding them.
cards.evidence_detail: Business opinion; no data.
cards.landing: Not a harness lever; supports maintaining the harness continually after each model release

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude Agent SDK is basically just wrapping the Claude Code CLI binary
cards.claim: The Agent SDK runs the same CLI, so behaviour matches if setting sources and flags are passed; the Max-plan terms mainly bar serving customers through the SDK or other harnesses.
cards.evidence_detail: His reading of recent terms changes, flagged by him as a gray area and not his own certainty.
cards.landing: If Workflow scripts or an Agent SDK pipeline are used, pass setting sources so project CLAUDE.md and skills load; check plan terms

gaps: Auto-captions are unlabelled by topic; Dex vs Vaibhav attribution was by content, so a few cards (R26-10, R26-15, R26-16, R26-18, R26-19, R26-41, R26-48) are Vaibhav's argument that Dex agrees with or proceeds on.
The PII episode is mostly Vaibhav on BAML and security; only a handful of Dex ideas were carded.
Whiteboard images in the README files were not viewed, so any content only drawn there (e.g. February probability-curve figure, skills whiteboards) is not captured.
The '37%' and '60%' context thresholds and the 10K tool-search threshold are spoken from memory, not verified against Claude Code docs.
Amazon senior-review policy is a secondhand news claim; not checked.
Inventory lists these three episodes only by number and title in a one-line entry, not by URL or content, so in_inventory true means title-level coverage.
